Narrowly
nar'ro-ly
adv. (with close scrutiny; with minute examination; closely)
From narrow, Saxon nearu, strait, close. To look narrowly is to look with the eye close in — the same figure as the English close inspection.

Biblical Definition

Both occurrences describe a searching examination, and in both the one examined would rather not be. Job complains of God's attention: “Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet” (Job 13:27). The picture is of a tracker following footprints, and Job experiences omniscience as surveillance — a man in the dark reads the same attribute as a threat that a man in the light reads as comfort. The second is the great taunt-song over the fallen king of Babylon: “They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms” (Isa 14:16). The dead crowd around and peer at him, leaning in to be sure it is really him. A tyrant who terrified the earth becomes an object of close inspection, and the verse is the answer to every accumulation of power. Set against Job's dread is David's invitation, which asks for the very thing Job resented: “Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts” (Psa 139:23).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines narrowly as with little breadth; contractedly; closely; accurately; with minute scrutiny; and nearly, within a little.

expand to see more

NAR'ROWLY, adv.

1. With little breadth.

2. Contractedly; without much extent.

3. Closely; accurately; with minute scrutiny; as, to look narrowly into an affair.

Thou lookest narrowly unto all my paths. Job 13. 4. Nearly; within a little; by a small distance; as, he narrowly escaped.

Key Scripture

Job 13:27 — "Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet."

Isaiah 14:16 — "They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms;"

Psalm 139:23 — "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:"

Hebrews 4:13 — "Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do."

Modern Corruption

Divine omniscience is experienced as surveillance and resented, or denied outright by open theism; Scripture presents it as the ground of both terror and comfort, depending on where a man stands.

expand to see more

Job 13:27 is honest about something devotional writing often avoids: being fully known is not automatically comforting. Job, in the dark and unable to account for his suffering, feels God's narrow looking as a man feels a tracker on his heels. The age has its own version, in which any absolute scrutiny is felt as a violation of autonomy, and the God who sees all is therefore an intolerable figure. Open theism offers the escape by denying exhaustive foreknowledge, and it is no escape at all — a God who does not know the end cannot be trusted with it, and Hebrews 4:13 is not negotiable: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.

What changes the experience is not the attribute but the standing. David asks for the identical scrutiny Job resents — search me, O God, and know my heart — because he is asking as a man in covenant, with nothing finally at stake in the verdict. That is the difference justification makes. And Isaiah 14:16 shows the attribute from the third side: the day comes when the men who could not be examined at all are looked at narrowly by everyone, and found to be very small. Omniscience is a terror to the guilty, a comfort to the covered, and a promise to everyone waiting for the tyrants to be seen plainly.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shamar (H8104), to watch, keep, observe closely; shaqaph (H8259), to look down and gaze; chaqar (H2713), to search out.

expand to see more

Hebrew tishmor (H8104) — thou watchest, guardest, observest; Job 13:27, the tracker's attention on every path.

Hebrew yashgichu (H7688) — they shall gaze intently, peer; Isaiah 14:16, the dead leaning in to look.

Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, explore to the bottom; Psalm 139:23, invited rather than resented.

Hebrew tithaqqeh — thou settest a print, engravest; Job 13:27, of the mark on the heels.

Saxon nearu — strait, close; Webster's root, the eye brought close in.

Usage

"“Lookest narrowly unto all my paths” — omniscience felt as a tracker on the heels."

"“They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee” — the tyrant, at last, inspected."

"“Search me, O God, and know my heart” — the same attribute, invited."
